headline: High: shared broad network and filesystem-capable pair can leak data and cascade errors; prompt-injection risk is limited by lack of a direct shared channel.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and Agent B reads/writes files and runs shell commands, but no direct shared channel is documented. The only plausible bridge is manual or file-based handoff, so injection risk exists but is not default-dangerous.
conditions: IF Agent A output is copied into files that Agent B later parses as instructions, injection becomes plausible.
IF an orchestrator adds a shared MCP or message queue between them, the risk increases.
mitigations: Keep handoffs manual and text-only.
Strip instructions from any file passed from A to B.
Use a read-only review step before B consumes A output.
Disable any shared MCP bridge unless provenance is tracked.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tags to inter-agent artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches session history, project code, and provider auth data while having broad network egress; Agent B reads/writes filesystem artifacts and certificate/private-key material. A shared workspace is not documented, but if one is introduced, either agent could expose sensitive data through networked outputs.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or mounted volume, leakage becomes plausible.
IF Agent A or B is given secrets in files, network egress can exfiltrate them.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mounts per agent.
Do not place secrets in shared directories.
Review outbound destinations before enabling network access.
Rotate any credentials exposed to either agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can spawn subprocesses and has full-permissions mode requested; Agent B can execute shell commands and write the filesystem. Even without documented shared state, overlapping write-adjacent capabilities create conflict if they target the same directory or container image.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory, they can overwrite each other's outputs.
IF either agent is granted the same mutable Docker or build context, race conditions become likely.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Run only one writer per target path.
Snapshot inputs before either agent mutates them.
Avoid sharing Docker build contexts.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce tool-assisted outputs and Agent B can execute shell actions, so A's output may be treated as authoritative by B. No verification step is documented, and uncertainty about the orchestration should be treated conservatively.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A output without validation, incorrect instructions can cascade into actions.
IF A is used to generate commands or facts that B then executes, downstream errors can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a human review gate between A and B.
Require B to validate commands before execution.
Log and diff A output before reuse.
Limit B to non-destructive commands by default.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles provider auth prompts and session history, while Agent B handles certificate private keys and registry credentials. Their documented data classes differ, so a shared workflow could mix sensitive material with different retention and handling expectations; no residency or certification mismatch is documented, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or credentials are processed in the same workflow, retention and handling controls must align.
IF either agent logs sensitive artifacts by default, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated secrets out of shared runs.
Disable verbose logging for secret-bearing tasks.
Separate retention policies by data class.
Review credential handling before execution.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries per agent.
